senses: A tool for basting meat with fat or gravy.
ety: From baste + -er.
examples: Hmm, yeah, but we didn’t have a turkey baster.

senses: The practice of drilling a hole in the skull as a physical, mental, or spiritual treatment.
ety: From New Latin trepanatio, formed from French trépan (“a drill”), itself from Latin trepanum, ultimately from Ancient Greek τρύπανον (trúpanon, “an auger, a drill”).
examples: According to the doctors, Lula, 79, underwent a trepanation: having a 3cm hole made in the skull to insert a drain to remove the bleeding.

senses: A raised earth mound, often topped with a wooden or stone structure and surrounded with a ditch.
An argument which is uncontroversial and easy to defend (in the context of a motte and bailey fallacy).
ety: From French motte, from Anglo-Norman/Old French motte (“mound, hillock”). Doublet of moat.
examples: The motte was a mound made of earth and surrounded by a ditch.

senses: An airy pudding served chilled, particularly chocolate mousse.
A savory dish, of meat or seafood, containing gelatin.
A styling cream used for hair.
A stable emulsion of water and oil that is created by wave action churning the water where an oil spill occurs.
ety: From French mousse (“foam, froth”), from Old French mosse (“moss”), from Frankish or Old Dutch *mosa (“moss”), from Proto-Germanic *musą (“moss, bog, marsh”). More at moss.
examples: He slicked his hair back with mousse, but the cowlick still stuck up.

Pretreatment of oil or sea water with dispersants or demulsifiers generally inhibits laboratory mousse formation with most of the oils and petroleum products tested (Berridge et al. , 1968b; Bridie et al. , 1980a,b).
When it washed ashore in Prince William Sound, the crude came in sticky gobs, in tar balls, in what they called mousse, crude whipped to a froth in the action of the sea.

senses: Moving or developing very slowly; tending to drag on; dull.
Typified by, or characteristic of, drag (women's clothing worn by men for the purpose of entertainment).
ety: From drag + -y.
examples: About two years ago I had been feeling tired and draggy for about six months. I went to find out what was going on. They told me I had Epstein-Barr.
The Who start off ramshackle, draggy even. They pick up while on a run of Tommy songs; by Amazing Journey they sound much more like the fizzing fathers of freak-beat.
The performer strode onto the stage wearing a glittery, draggy outfit.

senses: A fish that tends to take bait.
A person who takes up an offer or request.
ety: From Middle English biter, bitere, equivalent to bite + -er. Cognate with West Frisian biter (“biter”), Dutch bijter (“biter”), German Low German Bieter (“biter”), German Beißer (“biter”).
examples: She tried the same cast several times. I signaled her to switch flies. After two such changes we still couldn't move the fish. Some steelhead are biters; some are not.
I put up some fliers for the org but didn't get any biters

senses: To convert (sugar) into caramel.
To brown (sugar, or a foodstuff containing sugar) by means of heat.
To undergo this kind of conversion or browning.
ety: From caramel + -ize.
examples: Slowly cooking the onions will caramelize them, which brings out the sweetness and gives them a brown color.

senses: The currency of Haiti, divided into 100 centimes.
ety: From French, originally meaning “heavy, clumsy”. Cognate with Haitian Creole goud.
examples: Small boys eager to help in return for a gourd or two.

senses: A shrill noise, especially made by a voice or bird. If made by a bird, it typically signals discomfort or anger; a yell, scream, or call.
A complaint or objection.
The American night heron.
ety: First attested in 1821. Unknown, but probably of imitative origin (compare dialectal Italian squacco (“small-crested heron”) and English quack).
examples: That was the last roundup for McCutcheon’s Cresswell; it never moved from that field again. Not that there was any squawk from the landlord; the two of them owned it, of course.

senses: The Canadian dollar coin in common circulation since 1987.
The dollar as the Canadian unit of currency.
ety: From loon + -ie from the depiction of a loon on the reverse (tail-side) of the Canadian one-dollar coin.
examples: The loonie continued to rise against the greenback today.

senses: That has been given amnesty; whose past offences have been forgiven.
ety: From amnesty + -ed.
examples: The opening of the Panthéon Club in November 1795, a successor to the closed Jacobins, marked the beginnings of a recovery of the extra-parliamentary Left, now reinforced by amnestied militants.

senses: Making a clanking metallic sound.
Providing audible indication of imminent mechanical failure.
ety: From clank + -y.
examples: My father's first car was a clanky old Volkswagen Beetle.
The English band Crass sounded like a bag of rocks: scrabbly drum rolls, clanky guitars, no bass end, the words a jabbery Cockney caterwaul through endless stanzas of common meter.

senses: To make fun of (someone); to goad (a person) into responding, often in an aggressive manner.
ety: From Middle French tanter (“to tempt, try, provoke”), variant of Old French tempter (“to try”). Doublet of tempt.
examples: John taunts his brother to reveal his hiding spot.

senses: Having a single channel.
Having a single melodic line and no harmony.
Having simple one-to-one mapping between letters and phonemes.
ety: From mono- + -phonic. Compare Ancient Greek μονόφωνος (monóphōnos, “with only one voice or tone”)
examples: From a similar selection, says M. Remusat, the Coreans have made a monophonic alphabet of nine vowels and fifteen consonants, with which they write their language.

senses: A small village or hamlet, especially in the Highlands or Western Scotland.
ety: Borrowed from Scottish Gaelic clachan.
examples: But if you looked south in the dusty forenoon or at hot midday, you saw the far-off glimmer of a white road, the roofs of the ugly little clachan of Kilmaclavers, and the rigging of the fine new kirk of Threepdaidle.

senses: A young eel.
ety: Variant of eelfare, originally "brood of young eels", from Middle English *elfare, *elvare, from el (“eel”) + fare (“group of journeyers”). Equivalent to eel + fare. Liberman instead connects the second element of this word to a putative Old English suffix *-for(e), but there is no need to posit such a suffix when the traditional etymology suffices. Furthermore, such a suffix is not securely attested, and the spelling of the word's earliest attestation (as yele fare, ell vare) implies Middle English /aː/.
examples: When these glass eels enter freshwater they transform again into elvers – miniature versions of the adult eels.

senses: The quality of being sufficient, adequate or able to meet the needs.
ety: From adequ(ate) + -acy.
examples: His zeal is, of course, unquestionable; his adequacy, however, I doubt.
GREETINGS, adventurer! In honor of your adequacy, I bring you a gift from the Dunmer people!

senses: A person who steers the rear wheels of a fire truck (a tiller truck) or controls its ladder
ety: From tiller + -man.
examples: That function was reserved for the tillerman (the man that sits at the top steering position at the rear of the aerial ladder).
The driver in the back is called the tillerman. The tillerman steers the rear wheels, allowing the truck to turn onto narrow streets and alleys.

senses: A one-piece garment for an infant or small child, generally worn over a diaper.
A one-piece adult loungewear jumpsuit.
A one-piece fashionable streetwear worn mostly by teenagers.
ety: Genericized trademark from the Gerber Childrenswear brand name Onesies, which became reinterpreted as a plural. Equivalent to one + -sie.
examples: The Fever shared a video of the meeting on X (formerly known as Twitter), where an excited Clark got to hold the young baby and sign the youngster's onesie.

senses: To not select; to rule out of selection.
To reject (an incumbent) as a party's candidate for a forthcoming election.
ety: From de- + select.
examples: One recently deselected Sinn Féin assembly member, Davy Hyland in Newry and Armagh, has already quit the party in protest.

senses: A person who studies UFOs.
ety: From ufolog(y) + -ist. By surface analysis, UFO + -logist.
examples: Still, something strange was afoot in Rendlesham, and even if the file is unlikely to satisfy either ufologists or debunkers, it suggests that the truth is still out there.
But fear of abduction never stopped a good ufologist.

senses: Characterised by enthusiasm and a desire to communicate belief.
ety: From evangelist + -ic.
examples: I was pretty evangelistic about the merits of working in a small team.

senses: An ear or kernel of maize; in plural as mass noun: maize, corn.
ety: Borrowed from Afrikaans mielie, from obsolete Dutch milie (“millet, maize”), from Old French mil (“millet”).
examples: The wants of a native living with his tribe and cultivating mealies or Kafir corn are confined to a kaross (skin cloak) or some pieces of cotton cloth.
My mother planted and harvested her own mealies.

senses: Given to or marked by deliberate deceptiveness in behavior or speech.
ety: From duplicity + -ous.
examples: It reunites the horribly duplicitous skag-addicted non-heroes of the first movie about twentysomethings trying to get off heroin in Edinburgh, and finding that they have nothing very much to put in its place.

senses: Friendship; friendliness.
Mutual understanding and a peaceful relationship, especially between nations.
ety: From Middle English amite, from Old French amisté, amitie, amistiet, from Vulgar Latin *amīcitātem, derived from Latin amīcus (“friend”), from amō (“love”).
examples: To my native place ¶ Bent upon returning, ¶ Bosom all day burning ¶ To be where my race ¶ Well were known, 'twas much with me ¶ There to dwell in amity.

senses: Illuminated, lit.
ety: From kindle + -ing.
examples: The morning o'er the gilded grove Bright on the kindling landscape fell, I sought her where she oft did rove In want and sorrow's lonely cell;—

senses: Involving or relating to escalation.
ety: From escalate + -ory.
examples: The pattern of gradually increasing severity fits with the general image of an escalatory conflict model.
Is there an escalatory ladder in cyber, the same as with weapons of mass destruction?

senses: Personal, or distinctly personal; relating to the divine hypostases, or substances.
ety: Borrowed from Latin hypostaticus, from Ancient Greek ὑποστατικός (hupostatikós), from ὑποστατός (hupostatós). Equivalent to hypostasis + -tic.
examples: The hypostatic union, as it is called, the perfect and complete union of two whole and perfect natures in the person of Jesus Christ, underlies this apparent paradox

senses: A tall tower, often on a church, normally topped with a spire.
A high headdress of the 14th century.
ety: From Middle English stepel, from Old English stīpel, stȳpel, stīepel (“tower, steeple”), from Proto-West Germanic *staupil, from Proto-Germanic *staupilaz (“that which is steep, tower, steeple”), equivalent to steep + -le. Cognate with Old Norse stǫpull (“tower, steeple”).
examples: So, the woman and the child had gone by, and gone on, and five had sounded from the steeples.

senses: A heavy stick or club, usually used by policemen.
A martial art based on stick fighting originally practiced in India.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi लाठी (lāṭhī).
examples: A phalanx of policemen armed with lathis faced a mob of mill workers squatting on the road.
Lathi shares its basic principles with other martial arts.

senses: Chewing gum.
A chewable treat or toy intended for a pet.
ety: From chew + -ie.
examples: Also, I forgot to take my chewie out of my mouth.
The chewie would hide his smoker's breath and fool the teachers if they did a spot check.
Holding the chewie away from her, he encouraged the dog to walk up the ramp.

senses: Agreeing or harmonious; consistent (with).
ety: French concordant, from Latin concordans, present participle of concordare. See concord.
examples: Were every one employed in points concordant to their natures, professions, and arts, commonwealths would rise up of themselves.

senses: A dish made by browning grain, typically rice, in oil and then cooking it with a seasoned broth, to which meat and/or vegetables may be added.
ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish پلاو (modern Turkish pilav), from Classical Persian پلاو (pilāw), from Hindi पुलाव (pulāv)/Urdu پُلاؤ (pulāo), from Sauraseni Prakrit *𑀧𑀼𑀮𑀸𑀕 (*pulāga), from Sanskrit पुलाक (pulāka), which is probably of Dravidian origin. Akin to Tamil புழுக்கு (puḻukku, “cooked rice”). Doublet of pulao.
examples: My spirits rose as I passed among the tents and savored the aroma of steaming pots of pilaf and the long skewers of shashlyk roasting over the open fires.
Charlie Vaughn, the tribal chairman, dismissed his critics at the opening as people who are "eating tofu and pilaf and sitting in Phoenix with their plasma-screen TVs".

senses: A strong natural dislike or hatred; antipathy.
ety: From Ancient Greek ἀνταγωνιστής (antagōnistḗs, “opponent”), from ἀνταγωνίζομαι (antagōnízomai, “antagonize”), from ἀγών (agṓn, “contest”) (English agon).
examples: Their longstanding antagonism is manifested in frequent scuffles and shouting matches.

senses: Infected with one of the diseases known as leprosy.
Similar to leprosy or its symptoms.
Having the appearance of the skin of one infected with leprosy; flaking, peeling, scabby, scurfy.
Of gold or other metals: contaminated with other substances; impure.
ety: From Middle English leprous (“having leprosy or a skin disease with symptoms like leprosy; (alchemy) of metals or minerals: impure; a leper”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman leprous, lepros [and other forms], Middle French lepros, lepreux, and Old French leprous, lepros (“having leprosy; a leper”) (modern French lépreux), and from their etymon Late Latin leprosus (“having leprosy; (alchemy) of metals: impure; a leper”), from Latin lepra (“leprosy”) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of; overly; prone to’ forming adjectives from nouns). Lepra is derived from Ancient Greek λέπρᾱ (léprā, “leprosy
examples: And the Lord said furthermore unto him, Put now thine hand into thy bosom. And he put his hand into his bosom: and when he took it out, behold, his hand was leprous as snow.
And the cloud departed from off the tabernacle; and, behold, Miriam became leprous, white as snow: and Aaron looked upon Miriam, and, behold, she was leprous.

And why, except that it had moved everywhere with them and they regarded it as one of their possessions, had they kept the hatrack, its glass now leprous, most of its hooks broken, its woodwork ugly with painting-over?

senses: A mystic who follows quietism.
Someone who is not socially or politically active.
ety: From quiet + -ist, after Italian quietista.
examples: You need not give in to media clowns or dozing quietists.

senses: Clothing that is appropriate for both athletic and leisure pursuits.
ety: Blend of athletic + leisure.
examples: Of course, the athleisure category—infusing seemingly sporty clothes with a wear-it-all-day premise—has been booming for a while now.

senses: A soldier trained in special infiltration tactics.
A member of the Sturmabteilung, a Nazi street militia.
ety: A calque of German Sturmtruppen, from Sturm (“storm”) + Truppen (“troops”), equivalent to storm + trooper.
examples: Indeed, the infantry battle on the desolate ridgeline above Darwin would probably have seemed remarkably familiar to a World War I stormtrooper.
As you'll recall, the idea of the stormtrooper arose from the effort to break out of the trench warfare of World War I.
When he came upon such a scene he went up to a stormtrooper to protest.

senses: Jokey; inclined to or characterised by quipping.
ety: From quip + -y.
examples: I usually flinch at the quippy philosophies espoused on car bumper stickers...
One of them told us in a quippy comment: “we are not architects”.

senses: To pass a liquid through a porous substance; to filter.
To drain or seep through a porous substance.
To make (coffee) in a percolator.
(of coffee) to be prepared by percolation; (of a coffee pot) to brew coffee in this way.
To spread slowly or gradually; to slowly become noticed or realised.
ety: Borrowed from Latin percōlātus, perfect passive participle of percōlō (“to filter”), itself, from per (“through”) + cōlō (“to strain”) (from cōlum (“a strainer”), of unknown origin); see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix).
examples: Water percolates through sand.
Boiled, percolated, pressed, or filtered, black coffee ranges from a light tea-like drink to deep black brew.
Reports on the pitiful state of many prisons have finally percolated through to the Home Office, which has promised to look into the situation.
